page.text:
At the absolute bedrock of algebraic architecture lies the *magma* (also
known historically as a *groupoid* in Bourbaki's terminology, though
modern category theory reserves the word groupoid for a category whose
morphisms are all invertible). A magma consists of a carrier set $X$
equipped with a single binary operation $* : X \times X \to X$, subject
to no axiomatic constraints whatever beyond closure: combining any two
elements of $X$ produces an element of $X$.

Because magmas do not require associativity, the order of operations
matters critically: $(a * b) * c$ and $a * (b * c)$ may designate
completely disparate elements. Familiar examples of non-associative
magmas include the integers under subtraction, where
$(a - b) - c \neq a - (b - c)$ in general; the positive reals under
division; the octonions under multiplication; and parse trees in formal
languages under tree concatenation.
